ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description first: In the attached diagram, the left cylindrical glass is upright on a horizontal table and contains shaded water up to a dashed horizontal level. The right identical cylindrical glass is tilted and rests against the left glass; its shaded water surface lies on the same dashed horizontal level. In the tilted glass, that horizontal water level touches the circular bottom of the glass at exactly one upper point, while the lower visible point of that bottom is on the table. Reasoning: Let the common water height above the table be H. The base area is 3π cm^2, so if the base radius is r, then πr^2 = 3π, hence r = √3. Let A = 3π. The upright glass contains volume AH. For the tilted cylinder, let c be the vertical component of its axis direction. For a point of the bottom disk at height z, the water-filled length along the cylinder generator up to the horizontal water plane is (H - z)/c. Averaging over the circular bottom disk gives tilted water volume A(H - z_center)/c, where z_center is the height of the center of the tilted bottom disk. From the diagram, the lowest point of that bottom disk is on the table at height 0, and the highest point is tangent to the water level at height H. Therefore z_center = H/2. Thus the tilted water volume is A(H/2)/c. Since the two glasses contain the same amount of water, A(H/2)/c = AH, so c = 1/2. The vertical half-width of the tilted circular bottom disk is r√(1 - c^2). This equals H/2 because the bottom disk ranges vertically from 0 to H. Therefore H/2 = √3 · √(1 - 1/4) = √3 · √(3/4) = 3/2, so H = 3. The amount of water in each glass is AH = 3π · 3 = 9π cm^3.

method.method_draft: Use an axial cross-section route. From the image, take the vertical plane through the axis of the leaning cylinder and the tangent point on its bottom; in that plane the tilted glass appears as a parallelogram, and the circular bottom contributes a diameter whose lower endpoint is on the table and upper endpoint is exactly on the dashed water level. Image description: The attached diagram shows two identical cylindrical glasses. The left glass is upright on a horizontal table, with shaded water up to a dashed horizontal line. The right glass is tilted and rests against/near the upright glass; its shaded water surface is represented by the same dashed horizontal height. In the tilted glass, the dashed water line meets the bottom circle of the glass at exactly one point, as indicated in the diagram.

Reasoning: Use an axial cross-section through the axis of the tilted cylinder and the tangent point on its bottom. In this section, the tilted glass appears as a parallelogram. The circular base contributes a diameter in this cross-section; one endpoint is lowest, and the other endpoint is exactly at the dashed water level. Let the common water height be H. Since the base area is 3π cm², the radius satisfies πr² = 3π, so r = √3.

Let c be the vertical component of the tilted cylinder’s axis direction. Along generators of the tilted cylinder, the length filled with water varies linearly across the bottom disk: it is H/c at the lowest point and 0 at the tangent point at height H. Because the base disk is circular and the filled length is a linear function over it, the average filled generator length is the midpoint value, H/(2c). Thus the tilted-glass water volume is A · H/(2c), where A = 3π.

The upright glass has water volume A · H. The glasses contain equal amounts of water, so A · H/(2c) = A · H. Hence 1/(2c) = 1, so c = 1/2.

The bottom diameter is perpendicular to the cylinder axis, so its vertical projection is 2r√(1 - c²). This vertical projection equals the height H from the table to the dashed water line. Therefore H = 2r√(1 - 1/4) = 2√3 · √3/2 = 3.

So the water volume in each glass is A · H = 3π · 3 = 9π cm³.
